title: Requirements
description: Pin down what to build, how well it must work, and which trade-offs the product can live with.

lessons.title: Functional requirements
lessons.summary: Turn a vague prompt into a short list of testable features.

steps.prompt: The prompt is “Design a URL shortener.” Which question should you ask first?
options: Beyond shortening and redirecting, which features matter?
Should we use MySQL or Cassandra?
How should the short codes be generated?
Which cloud provider do you use?
steps.answer: Beyond shortening and redirecting, which features matter?
steps.why: Scale, API and data model are all designed around the features, so they come first. Databases and algorithms are answers to questions you haven't asked yet.

misconceptions.Should we use MySQL or Cassandra?: The database follows from the data and its access patterns, which depend on the features and scale.
misconceptions.How should the short codes be generated?: That's a deep dive. It only matters once you know what you're building and how many links you'll create.
misconceptions.Which cloud provider do you use?: The provider rarely changes the design. The requirements do.

steps.title: What the system does
steps.body: **Functional requirements** are behaviors users can see. Write each as a testable statement, “Users can …”, with a clear actor, action and result. If you can't imagine a test that passes or fails, it isn't a requirement yet. Keep the list short: three to five lines that define the product.

rows: Users can create a short link for any valid URL
Visiting a short link redirects to the original URL
Users can set an expiry date; expired links return 404

steps.prompt: Which is the crispest functional requirement for a photo app?
options: Users can upload photos easily
Users can upload photos quickly
Users can upload JPEG or PNG photos up to 20 MB
The system supports photo uploads
steps.answer: Users can upload JPEG or PNG photos up to 20 MB
steps.why: It names who acts, what they do, and limits you can test: a 21 MB file or a GIF should be rejected. The others hide the real requirement behind an adjective or a missing actor.

misconceptions.Users can upload photos easily: “Easily” can't be tested. Say exactly what the user can do.
misconceptions.Users can upload photos quickly: “Quickly” is about how well, which makes it non-functional, and it needs a number such as “p99 under 2 s”.
misconceptions.The system supports photo uploads: No actor and no limits: who uploads, in which formats, and how large?

steps.title: Scope in, scope out
steps.body: Nobody designs everything in 45 minutes, and real teams don't ship it all at once either. Pick the few features that define the product (the **MVP**, minimum viable product) and say out loud what you're leaving out. A short out-of-scope list shows judgment and saves your time for the parts that matter.

steps.context: Design a ride-hailing app. The interviewer says: “Focus on the core loop: getting a rider into a nearby driver's car.”
steps.prompt: Sort each feature for the MVP.

items.text: Riders can request a ride from their current location
Nearby drivers receive the request and can accept it
Riders can watch the matched driver approach on a map
items.why: Seeing the driver arrive is part of getting into the car, so it belongs to the core loop.

items.text: Riders can split the fare with friends
Drivers can download weekly earnings reports
Riders can book a ride a week in advance
items.why: Scheduling is a separate flow; the core loop is an on-demand request.

items.text: Riders earn loyalty points on every trip

steps.why: The interviewer named the core loop: request, match, pick-up. Everything else is real product work, but it's not what this design has to prove.

steps.title: Ask before you design
steps.body: Spend the first few minutes on questions whose answers change the design: **users** (who, and how many?), **features** (which few matter?), **scale** (reads and writes per second, data size) and **constraints** (latency, regions, compliance). Skip questions that wouldn't change anything, and write the answers down: they're your spec.

rows: Who uses it? How many daily?
Reads and writes per second? How much data?

steps.prompt: Match each clarifying question to the design decision it drives.
pairs: How many servers and how much storage
Whether to add caches and read replicas
Must users see their own post immediately?
Are users worldwide or in one country?
Whether to deploy in several regions
steps.why: A good question is one whose answer changes the architecture. If no answer would change what you draw, skip the question.

steps.text: “Users can share a post” is a [[functional]] requirement: it says [[what]] the system does. “Shared posts reach followers within 5 seconds” is a [[non-functional]] requirement: it says how [[well]] the system does it.
steps.why: Functional requirements are behaviors; non-functional ones are qualities with a number attached. The next lesson is about choosing those numbers.

lessons.title: Non-functional requirements
lessons.summary: How well it must work, in numbers you can measure.

steps.prompt: A service promises 99.9% availability. Roughly how much downtime does that allow per year?
options: About 9 minutes
About 1 hour
About 9 hours
About 4 days
steps.why: A year has about 8,760 hours, and 0.1% of that is about 8.8 hours. Each extra nine divides the budget by 10.

misconceptions.About 9 minutes: That's near five nines (99.999% allows about 5 minutes a year). Three nines is 0.1% of 8,760 hours.
misconceptions.About 1 hour: That's roughly 99.99% (about 53 minutes a year), ten times stricter.
misconceptions.About 4 days: That's 99% (about 3.7 days a year), ten times looser.

steps.title: How well, in numbers
steps.body: **Non-functional requirements** say how well the system must work: availability, latency, throughput, durability, consistency, scalability, security and cost. Each needs a number you could put on a dashboard or an alert. “Fast” is a wish; “p99 under 200 ms” is a requirement, and it also tells you when you're done.

right.title: Requirement
points: Acknowledged writes survive losing a data center

items.text: Users can follow other users
The home feed loads in under 300 ms at p99
Users can delete their own posts
The service stays up if a data center goes offline
items.why: That's availability: how well it keeps working, not a new feature.

items.text: Uploaded photos are never lost
items.why: Durability is a quality of how data is stored, not something a user does.

items.text: Users can search posts by hashtag
Infrastructure costs stay under $50K a month
Admins can suspend an account
items.why: An admin is still a user, and suspending an account is a behavior.

steps.why: Functional means what the system does for someone. Non-functional means how well it does it, measured by a number.

steps.title: Counting nines
steps.body: **Availability** is the share of time, or of requests, that the service works. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime 10× and costs more: redundancy, automatic failover, careful deploys. Pick the target the product needs: a payments system may justify four or five nines; an internal reporting tool doesn't.

steps.prompt: At 99.9% availability, how many minutes of downtime are allowed in a 30-day month?
steps.why: Teams manage this as a monthly **error budget**: at three nines, one bad deploy that takes 45 minutes to roll back spends the whole month's allowance.

steps.title: Every quality gets a number
steps.body: Each quality answers its own question. **Latency** targets are percentiles per operation, since averages hide slow tails. **Throughput** is a peak rate. **Durability** is the odds of losing data: Amazon S3 is designed for eleven nines a year. **Consistency** is how stale a read may be. Even **security** and **cost** get concrete targets.

rows: % of requests that succeed, per month
Peak requests or MB per second
Chance of losing an object per year
Headroom, e.g. 10× peak without a redesign
Rules you can audit, e.g. all data encrypted at rest
$ per month, or per million requests

steps.prompt: Match each quality to a measurable target.
pairs: No acknowledged write is ever lost
Reads reflect a write within 1 second
steps.why: Each target can be measured and alerted on. Availability and durability differ: a service can be down for an hour without losing a single byte.

options: Responses should be fast
Average response time is under 200 ms
99% of feed requests complete in under 200 ms
Every request completes in under 200 ms
steps.answer: 99% of feed requests complete in under 200 ms
steps.why: A percentile target is measurable and allows a small, explicit tail. It also names the operation, since a feed read and a video upload need different targets.

misconceptions.Responses should be fast: Not measurable: fast for which operation, and at what percentile?
misconceptions.Average response time is under 200 ms: An average can hide 5% of requests taking 3 seconds. Percentiles show the tail users feel.
misconceptions.Every request completes in under 200 ms: 100% is unachievable in practice: one garbage-collection pause or lost packet breaks it. Percentiles allow a small, explicit tail.

lessons.title: Access patterns and trade-offs
lessons.summary: Read/write mix, data growth, and what to give up when requirements collide.

steps.prompt: A URL shortener creates 100M links a month and serves 10B redirects a month. What should the design optimize for?
options: Fast redirects (reads)
Fast link creation (writes)
Both equally
The lowest storage cost
steps.why: Redirects outnumber creations 100 to 1, so read speed dominates both user experience and load. A create that takes 50 ms longer goes unnoticed; a slow redirect is felt on every click.

misconceptions.Fast link creation (writes): Only about 1 request in 100 is a write. Make writes correct; make reads fast.
misconceptions.Both equally: With a 100:1 ratio, a design tuned for reads handles far more of the real load.
misconceptions.The lowest storage cost: 100M links a month at a few hundred bytes each is tens of GB: cheap. Traffic is the hard part.

steps.title: Read-heavy or write-heavy?
steps.body: The **read:write ratio** shapes the design. **Read-heavy** systems (feeds, product pages, short links; often 100:1 or more) lean on caches, CDNs and read replicas. **Write-heavy** systems (logs, metrics, sensor data) need cheap appends, partitioned writes, and queues to absorb bursts. Ask for the ratio, or estimate it from how users behave.

left.title: Read-heavy
points: Cache hot data close to users

right.title: Write-heavy
points: Partition writes; buffer bursts in a queue

items.text: A news site's article pages
An application log collection pipeline
An online store's product catalog
Fitness trackers uploading heart rate every second
items.why: Millions of devices write constantly; each reading is rarely read, and then usually in aggregate.

items.text: Video playback on a streaming service
Click tracking for ad analytics
items.why: Every impression and click is recorded; reports read summaries, not raw rows.

steps.why: Ask who creates the data and who consumes it. Content made once and viewed many times is read-heavy; machine-generated events that are mostly aggregated later are write-heavy.

steps.title: How much data, how fast?
steps.body: Ask how big the data is and how fast it grows. 100M new posts a day at 1 KB each is 100 GB a day, about 36 TB a year before replication. Five years is around 180 TB, beyond a comfortable single database. Growth, not today's size, decides when you'll need to partition.

steps.prompt: A messaging app stores 10B messages a day, about 100 bytes each. How much new storage does it need per year, before replication?
solution: 1 TB × 365 ≈ 365 TB per year (about 1 PB with 3 replicas)
steps.why: Hundreds of terabytes a year rules out a single database server and points to a partitioned store built for appends. Saying “before replication” matters, because three copies triple it.

steps.title: When requirements collide
steps.body: Requirements can conflict. If replicas lose contact with each other (a network **partition**), each side must either refuse some requests to stay **consistent**, or keep answering with possibly stale data to stay **available**. That's the question the CAP theorem poses, and the product answers it, often per feature. The theory comes later in the course.

steps.context: A payments app has two features: account balances, and a social feed where friends can like each other's posts. A network partition splits its data centers.
steps.prompt: Which pairing of behaviors is right during the partition?
options: Balance: refuse withdrawals until it heals. Likes: accept them and reconcile later.
Balance: accept withdrawals and reconcile later. Likes: refuse them until it heals.
Both: accept writes and reconcile later.
Both: refuse writes until it heals.
steps.answer: Balance: refuse withdrawals until it heals. Likes: accept them and reconcile later.
steps.why: A wrong balance can let someone spend the same money twice, so refusing briefly is the safer failure. A like count that's off for a minute hurts no one, so staying available wins.

misconceptions.Balance: accept withdrawals and reconcil: Backwards. Reconciling balances later can allow double-spending, while refusing likes makes the app look broken to protect a number nobody audits.
Fine for likes, but two withdrawals on opposite sides of the partition could each see the full balance and both succeed.
Safe, but needlessly strict: rejecting likes makes the app look broken to protect a number nobody audits.

steps.prompt: A concert ticketing site sells reserved seats. During a network partition, should seat booking favor consistency or availability? Justify your choice in two or three sentences.
steps.hint: What's worse for a fan: an error message, or arriving to find someone else in their seat?

concepts.label: Prevents selling the same seat twice
Accepts that some requests fail or wait

steps.model: Favor consistency. If both sides of the partition kept selling, two fans could book the same seat, and a double-booking means refunds and angry customers at the door. It's better to reject or delay some booking requests with an error and let people retry once the partition heals.
steps.why: A double-sold seat is a real-world failure you can't quietly fix, while a brief “try again” is only an annoyance. A like count is the opposite case, where staying available wins.
